how-to-respond-to-a-chargeback.html.text:
Chargeback Evidence Packet Builder

How to respond to a chargeback

You get one submission. The reason code decides which records carry it — and the packet that wins a “merchandise not received” dispute is not the packet that wins a fraud claim.

Most small sellers lose winnable disputes the same way: they assemble whatever they can find, attach it all, and write a paragraph explaining that the customer is wrong. Reviewers work through these quickly, and a bundle that does not answer the specific question being asked reads as a bundle with no answer in it.

Every dispute arrives with a reason code. The code is the question. Everything else is your answer to it.

The seven questions behind seven common codes

Dispute reasonWhat the issuer is decidingRecords that carry the response
Merchandise not received Did the goods or services reach the buyer? Order confirmation, payment authorization, fulfilment or packing record, carrier tracking showing delivery
Credit not processed Was a promised refund actually issued — or did the policy the buyer accepted not entitle them to one? Order confirmation, payment authorization, refund or cancellation record, customer correspondence
Merchandise not as described What was the buyer shown before they paid? Order confirmation, the listing as it stood at purchase, customer correspondence, terms accepted at checkout
Fraudulent transaction Did the cardholder authorize this purchase? Payment authorization, AVS and CVV result, billing-to-shipping address match, delivery to that verified address
Duplicate transaction Were there two legitimate purchases, or one purchase billed twice? Order confirmation and payment authorization for each charge, tied to a distinct order
Subscription canceled Was the recurring charge still authorized when it posted, and how was it canceled? Subscription terms accepted at signup, payment authorization, any cancellation correspondence
Incorrect amount Does the amount charged match what the buyer agreed to pay? Order total as agreed, terms accepted at checkout, payment record showing what actually posted

Read the table across, not down. Tracking is the centre of a not-received response and close to irrelevant in a not-as-described one. The listing screenshot is the whole case for not-as-described and adds nothing to a fraud claim. Sellers who keep one “chargeback folder” template are sending the wrong records six times out of seven.

Four habits that decide the outcome before you write anything

1. Capture the listing before you edit it

A not-as-described dispute turns on what the product page said at the moment of purchase. If you have since fixed a typo, swapped a photo, or updated the dimensions, the current page is not evidence of anything. Save a copy of the listing when an order ships, or at minimum when a dispute lands — before you touch the page.

2. Keep the verification results, not just the outcome

“The payment went through” is not evidence in a fraud dispute; an unauthorized transaction also goes through. The AVS and CVV response codes are the part that speaks to authorization, and most gateways keep them on the transaction record rather than showing them in the order view. Find where yours stores them before you need them at speed.

3. Tie every record to this order

A tracking number in a screenshot with no order number beside it, an email thread with the subject line cropped out, a packing slip from a batch of forty: each of these is a record the reviewer cannot connect to the transaction in front of them. Same order ID visible on every page is worth more than three extra attachments.

4. Answer only the question asked

Two paragraphs of context about the buyer's tone, prior orders, or your refund philosophy does not help. State the facts, in order, with dates, and let the attachments do the work.

What does not belong in the submission

Your own gap list. It is genuinely useful to know that you never got a signature on delivery and that your correspondence with this buyer is thin — that is what tells you whether to fight the dispute at all, and what to fix before the next one. It belongs in your notes.

It does not belong in the file you send. A response that says “unfortunately we no longer have the original packing record” has volunteered the reason to decide against you. Say what you can support; attach what supports it; stop.

Personal data you were not asked for is the other category. Redact card numbers beyond the last four, unrelated customers' details in a shared screenshot, and anything in an email thread that has nothing to do with this order.

The deadline is your processor's, not the network's

Card networks publish outer limits, and articles quote them. Your processor's deadline is earlier, because they have to forward your response inside that limit, and it is the only one that matters to you. It is shown in your merchant account. On the last day, confirm the cutoff time and the timezone it is stated in — a deadline that reads as a date frequently expires mid-afternoon.

If the date has already passed, it is still worth contacting the processor rather than assuming nothing can be done. Sometimes there is a window; you will not find out by not asking.

Build the packet

The Chargeback Evidence Packet Builder puts the table above into a checklist that changes with the reason you pick, flags which core records you are missing, does the deadline arithmetic, and writes a factual response draft you can edit. It runs entirely in your browser — order details and notes are never uploaded — and it is free with no account.

Open the packet builder

Important boundary: This article and the tool it accompanies are an evidence organizer and drafting aid. They are not legal, financial, or payment-dispute advice, and they are not a statement of any processor's or card network's current rules. The tool does not predict a bank's decision and does not prove that a transaction was authorized. Processors differ, reason codes are re-mapped, and requirements change. Confirm what your processor asks for on your specific dispute, review every fact, and submit through their process before their deadline.

Common questions

What evidence should a small seller include in a chargeback response?

It depends on the reason code. A merchandise-not-received dispute is carried by the order record, the payment authorization, the fulfilment record, and carrier tracking showing delivery. A fraudulent-transaction dispute is carried by the authorization, the AVS and CVV result, the billing-to-shipping address match, and delivery to that verified address. Sending the same generic bundle to both wastes the one submission you get.

Should I explain in my response what evidence I could not find?

No. Keep the list of what you could not produce in your own working notes. The submission should state the facts you can support and attach the records that support them. An inventory of your gaps is useful to you and to nobody else who reads the file.

How long do I have to respond to a chargeback?

The deadline is set by your processor and shown in your merchant account, and it is usually shorter than the card network's outer limit because the processor needs time to forward the response. Work from the date in your dashboard, not from a figure quoted in an article, and confirm the local cutoff time on the final day.

Does winning a representment mean the dispute is over?

Not necessarily. An issuer can take some disputes to a second presentment or to arbitration, and the fee structure changes at each step. A clean, reason-matched packet at the first stage is what keeps the later stages from happening.

Chargeback response FAQ

What evidence should a small seller include?

Start with the order record, payment authorization, fulfillment record, and delivery or customer-contact evidence that relates to the dispute reason. This tool identifies a practical starting checklist; your processor may request different records.

Does this tool submit a chargeback response?

No. It runs in your browser and creates a reviewable draft. You remain responsible for checking the facts, redacting unnecessary personal data, meeting the processor's deadline, and submitting through the processor.

Can it guarantee that a dispute will be won?

No. The packet builder makes no prediction or legal determination. It only organizes the evidence you say you have and points out missing items in its checklist.

What extra evidence does a fraudulent-transaction dispute need that others don't?

The checklist's core set for "Fraudulent transaction" is the payment authorization, AVS/CVV verification result, billing-and-shipping address match, and carrier tracking — because the question there is whether the cardholder authorized the purchase, not whether the goods arrived. That is different from "Merchandise not received," where the core set is the order, payment, fulfillment record, and tracking, because the question is delivery. Device/login history and prior undisputed orders are recommended, not core, for a fraud claim.

How close to the deadline is too late to start?

The deadline field flags "urgent" once 3 days or fewer remain, and switches to a same-day warning when the deadline is today. If the date you enter has already passed, it tells you to contact the processor immediately rather than assume a filing is still possible — this tool only does the day-count arithmetic, it does not know your processor's actual cutoff time or whether a late submission is accepted. Start while the checklist still shows "ahead" so a missing record has time to be requested.

What if my dispute reason isn't one of the seven listed?

Choosing a reason outside the seven modeled ones falls back to a minimal core set — order confirmation and payment authorization — plus customer correspondence and accepted terms as recommended records, and a note to confirm the actual requirement with your processor for that reason code. The seven modeled reasons (merchandise not received, credit not processed, merchandise not as described, fraudulent transaction, duplicate transaction, subscription canceled, incorrect amount) cover the most common reason-code families, not every processor's exact taxonomy.

What evidence does a duplicate-charge, canceled-subscription, or wrong-amount dispute need?

A duplicate-transaction dispute is carried by the order and payment records for each charge, showing two distinct purchases rather than one purchase billed twice. A subscription-canceled dispute is carried by the terms the buyer accepted at signup and any record of when and how they canceled, because the question is whether the charge was still authorized when it posted. An incorrect-amount dispute is carried by the order total as originally agreed and the terms accepted at checkout, set against what was actually charged. None of these three share a core set with each other or with the original four.

vs-a-generic-dispute-checklist.html.text:
← Chargeback Evidence Packet Builder

This tool vs. a generic chargeback checklist

Search for “chargeback evidence checklist” and you get one list: order confirmation, proof of shipment or delivery, and a log of correspondence with the customer. Sellers bookmark that list and reuse it for every dispute that arrives, because it is free and it looks thorough. It is thorough for exactly one kind of dispute — merchandise not received — and silent about the other six reason codes a processor can post.

The card networks route a dispute under a reason code, and the reason code is the question a reviewer is actually deciding. This tool keeps a separate required-evidence set for each of the seven reasons it models, because a generic list answers only the delivery question and has no entry for the others.

Dispute reasonA generic checklist's usual fourWhat it is missing for this reason
Merchandise not received Order, shipping proof, correspondence, receipt Close enough — this is the case the generic list was written for.
Fraudulent transaction Order, shipping proof, correspondence, receipt AVS/CVV verification result and the billing-to-shipping address match — the actual question is authorization, not delivery.
Merchandise not as described Order, shipping proof, correspondence, receipt The product listing as shown at purchase and the terms accepted at checkout — the question is what the buyer was shown, not whether it arrived.
Subscription canceled Order, shipping proof, correspondence, receipt The signup terms and the cancellation record — there is no shipment in a subscription dispute at all.
Credit not processed Order, shipping proof, correspondence, receipt The refund or cancellation record itself — the question is whether a promised credit was issued, which shipping proof cannot answer.
Incorrect amount Order, shipping proof, correspondence, receipt The order total as originally agreed and the checkout terms — shipping proof says nothing about the price.
Duplicate transaction Order, shipping proof, correspondence, receipt Nothing extra, but two full order-and-payment pairs, one per charge — a single shipping record does not show two distinct purchases.

That is why a seller who reuses one checklist across reasons keeps attaching shipping proof to a fraud dispute — a record that answers a question nobody asked — while the AVS/CVV result the reviewer actually needed never makes it into the packet. This tool's checklist changes with the reason code you pick, so the gap it flags is the gap for that reason, not a copy-pasted generic one.

It is deliberately still just a checklist and a draft, not a submission service: nothing you type leaves your browser, there is no account, and it does not connect to your processor. The only thing it changes from a printed or bookmarked checklist is that it asks the reason first and tailors the list to it, and marks anything you have not checked off as a gap rather than letting a stale, wrong-reason list read as complete.

Common questions

What is wrong with using one chargeback checklist for every dispute?

The card networks group disputes into reason codes, and each reason code asks a different question. “Merchandise not received” asks whether the goods arrived, so it is carried by the order, payment authorization, fulfillment record, and delivery tracking. “Fraudulent transaction” asks whether the cardholder authorized the purchase at all, so it is carried by the payment authorization, the AVS/CVV verification result, the billing-to-shipping address match, and delivery to that verified address. A generic checklist built around receipts, shipping proof, and a correspondence log answers the first question and has nothing for the second — it does not mention AVS/CVV verification anywhere, because that record only matters for a fraud claim.

Does a generic checklist ever produce a complete packet?

Sometimes, by coincidence, for the reasons whose required records happen to overlap with what a generic list already covers — order and payment records appear in most of them. It reliably fails on the reasons that need something a generic list was never written to ask for: AVS/CVV verification for fraud, the accepted terms and cancellation record for a canceled-subscription dispute, or the product listing as shown at purchase for a not-as-described dispute.

Is this tool affiliated with any checklist or template site?

No. This page compares against the generic method of using a single downloaded or bookmarked chargeback checklist for every dispute, not any specific company or product.

Open the Chargeback Evidence Packet Builder and pick the dispute reason first — the checklist below it is the one built for that reason, not a generic one.

vs-chargeflow.html.text:
← Chargeback Evidence Packet Builder

This tool vs. Chargeflow

Chargeflow is a well-known automated chargeback-management platform, described on chargeflow.io as connecting directly to your payment processors and store to detect a dispute, pull relevant evidence — order details, shipping confirmations, delivery signatures, and more — and assemble and submit a card-network-compliant response automatically, with little or no manual work. It prices on a success basis: a percentage of whatever it recovers, rather than a flat subscription, and you can start it for free with no credit card.

That makes Chargeflow the right choice for one job: connecting to your systems so disputes are detected and responded to automatically, on an ongoing basis, without you assembling each packet by hand. This page does not do that job, and does not try to. It has no integrations, connects to no processor or store, and detects nothing on its own — it takes the facts you already have for one dispute and turns them into a reviewable checklist and draft.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I get disputes across many orders and want them detected and answered automatically, ongoing. Chargeflow or a comparable platform — that requires connecting your processor and store, and paying a share of what it recovers.
I have one dispute in front of me right now and the order, fulfillment, and delivery facts to back it. This tool — pick the dispute reason, check off what you hold, and get a reviewable draft in your browser, free, no signup.
I want a system that keeps working across every dispute without me touching it each time. Chargeflow or a comparable platform — this tool remembers nothing between disputes and connects to nothing.
I want to know exactly what evidence I am missing before I submit, without paying a percentage of the recovery. This tool's gap review, which marks what you do not yet hold as "do not submit" rather than guessing.

This tool is deliberately the opposite shape from an automated dispute-management platform: nothing to connect, no percentage of a recovery owed, and nothing you type ever leaves your browser. That makes it useful for a single dispute you already have facts for, and the wrong tool for detecting and answering disputes at volume across every order without manual review — that is exactly the job a platform like Chargeflow is built for.

It needs no account, no integration, and no sign-in: it is a static page, the checklist and draft run in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or a platform like Chargeflow?

They answer different questions. Chargeflow is a paid, automated dispute-management platform: it connects to your payment processors and store, pulls evidence such as order, shipping, and delivery data on its own, and submits card-network-compliant responses without you writing them, charging a percentage of whatever it recovers — described on Chargeflow's own site. That is an ongoing integration you connect once and let run. This tool does not connect to anything and recovers nothing on its own. It takes the order, fulfillment, delivery, and support facts you already have, walks you through the checklist your dispute reason actually needs, and gives you a draft to review and submit yourself, in your browser, for free.

Is this page affiliated with Chargeflow?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Chargeflow. Chargeflow is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on Chargeflow's own public site.
